learningObjectives: Explain or demonstrate the main idea: natural notes on low e and a.

explanation.keyIdea: The fretboard is a repeating pitch map. Each adjacent fret is one semitone. The natural-note sequence repeats A–G; B–C and E–F are adjacent semitones. Octave shapes connect the same note name in different positions.
explanation.plainLanguage: This lesson focuses on natural notes on low e and a. First understand the sound or movement, then practise a small part, then return to the musical whole. Treat the written checkpoint as an observable target, not a deadline.

lessons.title: Triad inversions
lessons.focus: Major triad root position and inversions on the top string set
learningObjectives: Explain the difference between root position and triad inversions.
Play the three inversions of the selected major triad on the top string set.
Identify the root and the lowest chord tone in each voicing, then connect the shapes in a short progression.

explanation.keyIdea: A triad inversion reorders the same root, third and fifth so a different chord tone is lowest. Identifying the lowest note helps name the inversion and connects fretboard shapes to harmonic function.
explanation.plainLanguage: Keep the same three chord tones, change which one is lowest, and name the inversion. Do not confuse a triad inversion with a new chord quality.
explanation.workedExample: Use the C major triad references on the top string set. Play root position, then move the notes to place the third and fifth as the lowest chord tone in turn.

demonstrationOrReference.referenceSuggestion: Use GuitarLab's original chord, fretboard or rhythm examples and demonstrate the exact task described here. Keep the task adaptable to the learner's instrument, experience and comfort; do not rely on copied commercial tabs or recordings.
steps: Name the root, third and fifth of the selected major triad.
Play the root-position voicing on the top string set and identify the lowest chord tone.
Revoice the same three notes so the third becomes the lowest note; name the first inversion.
Revoice the same notes so the fifth becomes the lowest note; name the second inversion.
Move between the three voicings while listening for the same major quality.
